articles.title: SC upholds constitutionality of law extending Barangay, SK officials' terms
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has upheld the constitutionality of the law extending the term of office of Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials to five years, while scheduling the next Barangay…

blocks.text: The Supreme Court (SC) has upheld the constitutionality of the law extending the term of office of Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials to five years, while scheduling the next Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) for November 2028.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act No. 12326 into law in September, which effectively postponed the BSKE, established the five-year term, and rescheduled the polls to 2028.
In a 33-page decision, the High Court dismissed the petition filed by election lawyer Romulo Macalintal challenging the constitutionality of the law.

The SC stated that the law's primary purpose is to set the term of office rather than to postpone the election, and therefore the guidelines established in the 2023 Macalintal decision—cited by the petitioner—do not apply.

“It sets a new five-year interval between elections. Its principal purpose, as gleaned from its text, is to fix the term of barangay and SK officials. Setting the next BSKE for November 2028 implements the new term, and is not an independent objective,” the decision read.

The High Court noted that rescheduling the BSKE to November 2028 merely implements the new term, adding that an adjustment to the election schedule does not automatically classify the legislation as an election postponement law.
The SC also underscored Congress's power to fix, modify, and extend the term of barangay officials as necessary, provided the transition period before the new term takes effect remains reasonable.

With incumbent barangay officials having been elected on October 30, 2023, the Court found the November 2028 schedule reasonable, not unduly long, and consistent with the five-year term prescribed under RA 12326.

Additionally, the Court considered lawmakers' concerns that conducting the BSKE in 2027 could disrupt the Commission on Elections’ preparations for the May 2028 National and Local Elections, while a five-year cycle starting in 2026 would cause future BSKEs to overlap with the 2031 national polls.

The High Court also rejected the argument that the law infringes upon the public's right to vote, emphasizing that the key requirement of suffrage is that elections take place regularly at fixed and predictable intervals established by law.

“Republic Act No. 12232 did not abolish or indefinitely postpone the BSKE but changed the statutory term and established a new and definite electoral cycle. We ruled that such legislation did not violate the right of suffrage,” the court said.

Finally, the SC clarified that the law does not grant incumbent officials a new term, but rather allows them to remain in office in a holdover capacity, which does not constitute a legislative appointment.

“The incumbents themselves were elected in the October 2023 BKSE. Their continuation in office pending the election of their successors is not an appointment by Congress, but the operation of a hold-over provision that the Court has repeatedly sustained,” the decision noted.

Macalintal previously filed a petition seeking the issuance of a temporary restraining order or a status quo ante order directing the Office of the President, through the Executive Secretary, the Senate, the House of Representatives, and the Commission on Elections (Comelec) to refrain from implementing RA No. 12326. He also asked the SC to declare the law inoperative, invalid, and/or unconstitutional insofar as it pertains to the postponement of the BSKE.

Accordingly, the SC denied Macalintal’s prayer for the issuance of a temporary restraining order, status quo ante order, and/or writ of preliminary injunction against the law, ultimately dismissing his petition for lack of merit.
The decision was penned by then Associate Justice Rodil V. Zalameda and promulgated on October 14, 2026.
Comelec
For its part, the Comelec expressed its appreciation for the prompt resolution of the issue, clearing any doubts about the constitutionality of the term-fixing law.

“Although not unanimous, the SC decision is already a jurisprudence forming part of the law of the land. Our deepest appreciation to the highest court for resolving promptly the controversy and clearing any doubt as to the legality of the law,” Comelec Chairman George Erwin Garcia told reporters in a message.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows
articles.summary: YouGov survey finds support for tree planting and emissions taxes but opposition to air travel and fuel levies

blocks.text: Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.

The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate breakdown through the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and destructive storms.

Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.

Those in the EU were more likely to say that climate action decisions should be made at EU rather than national level, a feeling shared by 50-54% of respondents in France, Italy and Germany as well as 61% in Denmark and 64% in Spain.

Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”. YouGov noted an uptick in concern during this summer’s heatwaves.
In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.

The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month. Concern in other countries spiked in August but has since dipped.

In Germany, for example, the number very concerned rose from 27% in April to 40% in August but has now fallen back to 31%. Concern remained relatively stable in Denmark, at 66%-69% “worried” and 20%-23% “very worried”.

Across the six countries surveyed, respondents mostly (45%-63%) thought it was not too late to avert the worst impacts of the climate crisis but that it would require a drastic change in approach. Only 11%-24% believed it was already too late.
after newsletter promotion

Between 9% and 20% said they thought current measures would be enough to prevent the most serious impacts. But in terms of what climate actions had support, those not directly affecting people’s lives were the most popular.

Measures such as planting more trees, subsidising energy efficiency, banning single-use plastics and taxing big emitters were all favoured, while increasing fuel duty, limiting meat and dairy, taxing air fares and banning new petrol and diesel cars were opposed.

A similar pattern emerged when respondents were asked what steps they would be prepared to take: cheap and easy actions such as creating green space at home and eating only seasonal fruit and vegetables were popular, but not shopping exclusively secondhand or paying more for flights.

articles.title: Death toll from Russian attack in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region climbs to 53
articles.summary: The death toll from Russia's bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday has risen to 53, the acting regional governor said Friday, making it one of…

image.caption: In a picture released Friday by the State Emergency Service of Ukraine, a rescuer searches for the bodies of residents at the site of an underground shelter in the compound of a local school, which was used as a humanitarian aid hub, in the front-line town of Komyshuvakha. It was hit earlier this we

blocks.text: World

The death toll from Russia's bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday has risen to 53, the acting regional governor said Friday, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.
Russia confirms new attacks, hours after Kremlin officials met at White House event led by Melania Trump

In a post on the Telegram messaging app, Mykhailo Semikin said search and rescue work at the site in the village of Komyshuvakha had entered its fifth day. Ukraine's Emergency Service had earlier said the toll was 50 and that search and rescue work was continuing despite difficult conditions and the constant threat of repeat Russian strikes.

Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure caused new power outages overnight and on Friday morning in seven Ukrainian regions, Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said. The affected regions were Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Chernihiv.
"The situation remains most difficult in the capital region," Nekrasov said, adding that utility workers were still having to impose network restrictions because of heavy damage.
How involved is Melania Trump in the push for peace in Ukraine?

The Russian military admitted it struck an energy storage battery facility in Ukraine's Kyiv region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea port of Odesa, with its Defence Ministry claiming on Telegram Friday that both were being used for military purposes.

The attacks came a day after several Russian and Ukrainian officials gathered at the White House in a meeting organized by Melania Trump to mark a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. Nearly 800 people were escorted from the small city in a pause in fighting the U.S. first lady helped broker.

items: Melania Trump hosted officials from Russia and Ukraine. Just what's behind her peace push?

blocks.text: "It was a very positive meeting, and the main thing is that the positive outlook and willingness to continue such humanitarian work is maintained," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Friday.

Ukrainian officials also praised Melania Trump's efforts, which have also included work to help Ukrainian children deported or forcibly moved from Russian-occupied territory. A presidential decree this week signed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy cited her "significant personal contribution" to humanitarian support for Ukraine in the award known as the Order of Princess Olga, 1st class.
Trump optimistic ahead of Abu Dhabi talks
Russia was led at the White House meeting by Kirill Dmitriev, envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

U.S. President Donald Trump confirmed he met privately with Dmitriev on Thursday, but would not disclose what was discussed. The U.S., Ukraine and Russia will hold talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates early next week as the war nears the five-year mark.
Pedestrians walk down a dark street during a power outage following attacks in Kyiv late Thursday. (Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images)
Trump, speaking to reporters at the White House, said the war was close to being settled and that ending it might involve all of Europe.

"It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine.… I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled," Trump said.
Trump has frequently predicted an agreement to end Europe's deadliest conflict since the Second World War since returning to the presidency in early 2025.

items: Putin pushes the myth of Russian invincibility, seemingly to set his terms for peace

blocks.text: The U.S. president also spoke to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday, the government in Berlin said.

The call between Merz and ⁠Trump ⁠took place "against ​the backdrop of long-standing preparations regarding the ​format ⁠of negotiations in Abu Dhabi or, at a later date, in other locations," the German government spokesperson said.

While Trump's Republican Party performed badly in the recent U.S. midterms, he will be president for two more years and able to influence what is happening in Ukraine. Moscow hopes Trump can pressure Kyiv into agreeing a deal that meets many of its conditions, such as full Russian control of Ukraine's Donbas region and a bar on Ukraine joining NATO.
Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.

articles.title: Tanzania: Opposition leader Tundu Lissu jailed for four years
articles.summary: Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu has been sentenced to four years in prison after being cleared of treason. Lissu condemned his conviction for incitement, which had not been among the charges…

image.caption: Lissu had already spent 19 months in jail before receiving his four-year sentence (FILE: 19/05/2025)Image: Ericky Boniphase/DW

blocks.text: Tundu Lissu, the leader of Tanzania's main opposition party, was sentenced to four years in prison on Friday for incitement to unrest after being cleared of treason.
While the verdict removed the threat of a death sentence, judges convicted Lissu of an offense that was not among the charges he faced.
What did the court decide?
Judges found that Chadema leader Lissu's statements about blocking the election were intended to disrupt the vote and encourage violence.
"We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence," the judge said.
Lissu disputed his conviction on a charge different from the treason accusation he had faced.
"I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles," he said, apparently referring to President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

Lissu was arrested in April 2025 over a speech in which prosecutors said he told supporters the opposition would "block the election" and "mobilize rebellion." He pleaded not guilty, arguing that his speech broke no law and that the prosecution was politically motivated. Lissu has already spent 19 months in jail.
The Tanzania voter boycott over opposition party exclusion
"All this was political persecution. Excuses were created to imprison me," he told the court after the verdict.
How did the case fuel Tanzania's unrest?
Lissu's arrest, alleged abductions of government critics, and Chadema's exclusion from the October 2025 election helped drive protests across the country.
Hundreds died as police opened fire on protesters in several cities. Opposition figures and rights groups put the toll in the thousands.

A commission appointed by President Samia Suluhu Hassan reported in April that at least 518 people had been killed and blamed protesters for the violence. The government denied allegations that security forces used excessive force.
Security was tightened in the commercial capital, Dar es Salaam, and around the courthouse ahead of Friday's verdict.
Why has the trial drawn international criticism?
British and European Union lawmakers described the case as politically motivated and called for Lissu's immediate release.
"The use of capital punishment against a political opponent risks turning the justice system into an instrument of political repression," they wrote to Hassan.
Meet Tundu Lissu: The leader of Tanzania's Chadema party
Lissu, 58, has been repeatedly arrested for opposing the government. In 2017, he survived an assassination attempt in which he was shot 16 times. He believes the attack was politically motivated.

articles.title: "No choice but to bear it": Delhi's unrelenting air pollution crisis
articles.summary: Despite years of government interventions, emergency restrictions and public outrage, Delhi continues to battle dangerously polluted air every winter. Why isn't there a lasting solution to a…

image.caption: Experts say restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels [FILE: November 9, 2025]Image: Arvind Yadav/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: On a slightly chilly and distinctly smoggy morning in New Delhi, Khushboo Arora was looking for another air purifier for her mother, who has underlying health complications, before the city's air quality deteriorated further.

"Already, I am starting to get a recurring headache," she said. "These days when I wake up, I don't feel fresh. As the day progresses, I feel a heaviness in my head, itching in my eye and a constantly parched throat."
Not too long ago, the unpacking of woolens announced the advent of winter in Delhi. Now, it's the light hum of an air purifier in the corner.

Arora said she has already stopped doing yoga in the park and taking her morning walks. She has also filled her house with air-purifying plants and started spraying water mist inside the house to bring down the level of pollution.
"My parents look at me like I have gone mad. But I feel people are not realizing the gravity of the situation," she said.
A recurring crisis

Winters in Delhi increasingly follow a familiar pattern: Air quality deteriorates, residents struggle to breathe, emergency restrictions kick in and governments exchange blame. Then the season changes, only for the cycle to repeat the following year.

On Thursday, Delhi's air fell into the "Very unhealthy" category, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir, with an average PM2.5 concentration of 157.9 micrograms per cubic meter of air. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends an annual safe limit of no more than 5 micrograms.

Studies have shown that exposure to PM2.5 — air particles with a diameter smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream — is associated with an increased incidence of head and neck cancer (HNC), like oral, nasal and throat cancers.
But despite years of attempted interventions, India's capital continues to struggle with the same pollution crisis.

blocks.caption: The issue has persisted for years despite public outrage [FILE: November 6, 2025]Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is causing the air pollution?
Delhi is not dealing with an unknown problem. There is considerable scientific understanding of its causes.

A 2026 assessment by an expert panel reviewed by the Delhi government identified the major winter contributors of PM2.5 as vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road and construction dust, biomass and waste burning, and pollution from neighboring regions.

Sunil Dahiya, founder of the environmental group EnviroCatalysts, said Delhi is part of a larger airshed. On most winter days, more pollution comes into Delhi than is generated inside it, according to the environmentalist.

"Analysis of the government's Decision Support System (DSS) data for winter 2025 found that around 65% of Delhi's PM2.5 came from outside the city and about 35% from sources within it," he told DW, adding that neighboring Noida and Gurugram, which comprise the National Capital Region (NCR), are some of the biggest contributors.
Coordinating action across the NCR, which spans Delhi and parts of three neighboring states, remains a major obstacle.
"This is a shared problem, and no single city can solve it alone," Dahiya said.
Why aren't anti-pollution policies working?
To understand why existing policies have not delivered sustained improvements, Dahiya highlighted the gap between scientific recommendations and state action.
"Scientists have said for over a decade that we need airshed-wide, year-round, source-specific action. What we mostly get is seasonal and reactive," he said.

According to the environmentalist, emergency restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels. Short-term measures such as water sprinklers and smog towers provide little relief, while bigger structural changes are slow to materialize. These include stricter enforcement of industrial emissions, cleaner fuels, expanded public transport, vehicle electrification and viable alternatives to crop burning for farmers.

blocks.caption: Delhi has imposed restrictions on vehicles under a certain emission standard [FILE: December 19, 2025]Image: Sunil Ghosh/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The science is not the bottleneck. Implementation, regional coordination and political will are," said Dahiya. "Until targets are tied to emission reductions at each source, and someone is held accountable for meeting them, we will keep having the same conversation every November."
Bhavreen Kandhari, co-founder of Warrior Moms, agrees that official responses focus on reacting rather than preventing.

"They allow pollution to occur and then try to clean it up — producing nice photo opportunities of water sprinklers and smog guns, or talking about cloud seeding," Kandhari told DW. "Creating pollution only to clean it up later is a waste of public funds, time, and health."
Kandhari also added that incinerating waste instead of proper waste management has only exacerbated the situation.
The politics of pollution
Another obstacle to a lasting solution has been the political blame game that starts as soon as the air quality worsens.

On Thursday, Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said stubble-burning in the neighboring state of Punjab is contributing to the capital's rising pollution, according to public broadcaster All India Radio. He insisted that in Delhi, construction, vehicle and industrial sources were controlled.

Dahiya agreed that seasonal crop-burning fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana "is an episodic but sharp contributor" which "can tip 'very poor' air into 'severe'" for a few weeks. But it is not the lone contributor.

"Among sources within Delhi, vehicles alone contribute roughly 51-53% of local PM2.5. A large share of winter PM2.5 is also secondary particulate formed from gases like sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia," Dahiya said. "That points straight back to combustion in power plants, industry and transport."
"If stubble burning ended tomorrow, Delhi would still breathe unhealthy air for most of the year," he added.
DW reached out to several Delhi government officials for a response, but received no reply.
What needs to change?
Delhi is also home to millions of people who cannot afford air purifiers and have no escape from the toxic air.
Among them is Deepika, who works as domestic help in an affluent South Delhi neighborhood. She has been coughing for a week.
It is the same every year, she said.
"I have no choice but to bear it for the next few months."

blocks.caption: Water sprinklers and smog towers provide some relief but experts say deeper reform is needed [FILE: December 16, 2025]Image: Arun Sankar/AFP

blocks.text: The people DW spoke to point to a common set of priorities: Addressing Delhi's pollution crisis requires year-round pollution control rather than seasonal restrictions, better coordination between governments and stronger enforcement of existing regulations and measurable targets. They say the city needs a sustained clean-air strategy more than another winter emergency plan.
Namrata Yadav is a Delhi resident and the mother of an eight-year-old boy. They both joined protests against air pollution in November. A year later, the problems persist.
"It is exhausting to repeat the same things year after year, only to be dismissed as paranoid or alarmist for demanding something as basic as clean air," she said.

Calling for lasting solutions driven by science, policy and accountability, Yadav said: "We have spent years learning how to live with pollution. It is time we demanded that those responsible learn how to end it."
Smog chokes New Delhi despite India's push against pollution

articles.title: Kenya cult leader Paul Mackenzie sentenced to 200 years
articles.summary: A court in Kenya has sentenced Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and an adult. He told them to starve themselves to death as part of his apocalyptic religious cult.

image.caption: Paul Mackenzie was convicted earlier this year, and could potentially have faced the death sentence Image: Luis Tato/AFP

blocks.text: Kenyan religious sect leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday, at the culmination of a trial following the discovery of hundreds of corpses in the woods.

A self-proclaimed pastor and longstanding leader of a new age Christian apocalyptic cult called the Good News International Church, Mackenzie was convicted in October of 191 counts of murder in the deaths of one adult and 190 children.
Justice Diana Kavedza said the sentence was comprised of 100 years for 183 counts of murder by starvation and another 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide.
He could have faced the death penalty, which is still technically on the books in Kenya.
However, like several countries that have kept capital punishment in their legal code but stopped actually using it, Kenya has not executed anybody since 1987.

While the charges against Mackenzie pertained to 191 deaths, some 400 people were found dead in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie's so-called church had been operating since 2003, based in the coastal town of Malindi.
Mackenzie had denied the charges, saying that he did not force the cult followers to starve.
A total of 28 accomplices were given various prison sentences for their roles in the deaths.
Shakahola and Boko Haram: Countering extremism with education

articles.title: ‘An abomination’: Idaho hunters earned thousands of dollars to kill newborn wolf pups, records reveal
articles.summary:
Wildlife advocates incensed as documents show state paid out $2,000 per kill in effort to shrink state’s wolf population

Idaho officials paid hunters thousands of dollars for killing a dozen…

blocks.text: Idaho officials paid hunters thousands of dollars for killing a dozen newborn wolf pups this spring, including what appears to be at least one full litter killed in or near its den, according to state records shared with the Guardian and Public Domain.

The wolf pup killings have incensed wildlife advocates in Idaho, where state wildlife officials have been ordered to take extraordinary measures to shrink the state’s re-introduced wolf population amid complaints from the livestock industry and big game hunting outfitters.

A law passed five years ago by the Republican-dominated state legislature loosened restrictions on hunting seasons, removed restrictions on killing methods and allowed people to contract third parties to kill wolves. Individual hunters and trappers are able to buy an unlimited number of permits to kill wolves, which cost $14 each for state residents and $32 for non-residents.

In 2021, Idaho game officials also entered into an agreement with the Foundation for Wildlife Management, a non-profit devoted to reducing wolves to help boost deer and elk numbers, to reimburse expenses to any hunter and trapper who provides proof of killing a wolf. The program pays for a wide range of expenses, including truck payments, fuel, ammunition and outdoor clothing.

blocks.caption: A protest against wolves in Montana and Idaho in September 2011. Photograph: William Campbell/Corbis/Getty Images

blocks.text: The reimbursement program paid $2,000 per wolf kill through the hunting season that ended in June, including the 12 pups, records from the state’s fish and game agency show. The program is funded with a mix of taxpayer money, hunting license sales and contributions from the Foundation for Wildlife Management. .

“It’s an abomination,” said Brooks Fahy, director of the advocacy group Predator Defense. “I think most people, even in Idaho, if they actually understood the depth of this, the fact that taxpayer dollars are paying for this – they would be appalled.”

“Let’s call this what it is – it’s a goddamned bounty,” Fahy said. “What kind of receipts are you going to show for 12 pups who weigh 12lbs? It’s ridiculous on its face and the state of Idaho should be ashamed.”
Neither the foundation nor the Idaho wolf depredation control board, a government entity that oversees payments for third-party wolf killings, responded to requests for comment.

Gray wolves were all but wiped off the map in the continental United States by the mid-20th century through government extermination programs, but the population has rebounded in Idaho since being reintroduced by the US Fish and Wildlife Service in 1995. That has reignited tensions with ranchers and big game outfitters whose livelihoods are affected by the animals.

blocks.caption: Sawtooth Mountains, Idaho. A gray wolf peers from behind a bush. Photograph: Jim and Jamie Dutcher/Getty Images/National Geographic

blocks.text: Three separate hunters used rifles to kill a total of 12 wolf pups in Idaho’s northern panhandle region on April 25, the records show – though in at least two instances the records also include a contradictory statement saying that “no weapon” was used. The pups were likely between one and three weeks old by that date. Wolves give birth once a year in the spring.

Hunters and trappers must present a skull and hide with proof of sex attached to a wildlife officer for every wolf killed in the state. The officer normally takes a tooth sample, which allows state biologists to estimate the animal’s age and genetic information.
Officers did not take teeth samples from the 12 pups, however – likely because their teeth had yet to grow in or were too small to extract, according to Idaho fish and game biologist Cory Mosby.

Mosby confirmed that the 12 wolves documented in the records were pups. No state regulation bars the killing of pups, he said. Wildlife officials would normally restrict killing pups by closing the hunting and trapping seasons during the spring, when wolves typically give birth.

But the state management plan, adopted in 2023, mandates culling wolves to about 650 animals in spring, when wolf numbers typically peak. The state’s permissive hunting and trapping regulations, including the yearlong season, are designed to tamp wolf numbers down to that target and will likely become more restrictive as the population dwindles, Mosby said.

That day remains a long way away. Idaho wildlife authorities estimate that the population peaked at about 1,600 wolves in spring back in 2019. That figure for this year still stood at more than 1,100 wolves, despite aggressive hunting and trapping and state-backed payments to incentivize wolf killings. Mosby said that hitting the target would require consistently killing more than a third of the wolf population annually.

“They’re an incredibly impressive and resilient species,” Mosby said. “It takes sustained, high levels of harvest to get into what you call ‘additive’ mortality – where you’re actually removing animals.”
Fishing wolves from dens
The records state that all 12 wolf pups were killed by “still stalk” – a method in which hunters spot an animal and then sneak up on it to take a shot.
But wolf experts said that the hunters responsible had more likely located the dens, monitored them until the mothers had given birth, then pulled the pups out to kill them.

The tactic of fishing wild canine pups from dens has a long history in the American west, where livestock interests have historically clashed with wolves and coyotes. Modern trail cameras with cellular technology make it far easier to watch over dens, said Carter Niemeyer, who spent nearly three decades working at the US Department of Agriculture’s wildlife services, an agency charged with lethal removal of animals that prey on livestock.

blocks.caption: Angus cows and calves are seen through dead sage brush as they graze on native and non-native grasses in eastern Idaho. Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Killing six wolves or 12 wolves total all on the same day by stalking – that doesn’t happen,” Niemeyer said. “Never heard of it.”

“It would be easy to determine when a female had her pups by her physical appearance going in and out of her den,” Niemeyer added. “I think the public should be outraged by it and sportsmen should be outraged by it too. I’m a sportsman and that’s stooping pretty low – collecting bounties on wolf pups.”

Doug Smith, a biologist who oversaw the wolf program at Yellowstone national park, said he has pulled wolf pups out of dens for research purposes. The parents don’t usually protect their young. Instead, they scurry off about 50 yards away and bark.
“It’s easy to do,” Smith said. “If you can’t reach them, you dig them out with a shovel.”

Smith raised concerns about killing whole litters, however. Wolves travel more independently in the summer and use the den to regroup later in the year. Killing a whole litter could fracture a pack or dissolve it entirely, he said.
“Wolves breed once a year, so the birth of the pups is a very important thing,” Smith said. “The pack’s life hinges on those pups. They’re the glue that holds the pack together.”
Renewed attacks from the White House

Gray wolves remain protected by the Endangered Species Act in most of the continental United States. But the northern Rocky states of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming have all secured state management of wolves since their reintroduction to the region in the 1990s. All three states have pursued aggressive tactics to beat their numbers back.

Idaho hunters and trappers have targeted wolf pups in the past. Hunters killed three pups with rifle shots in the same region two years ago, according to a report from the Idaho Statesman. Federal wildlife control officers killed eight wolf pups from Idaho’s Timberline pack outside Boise back in 2021 to avoid conflict with a rancher, drawing condemnation from wolf advocates, environmental groups and local students who had adopted the pack as their high school mascot.

blocks.caption: Bill Ross, a handler with the Wolf People education organization, in Spirit Lake, Idaho in 2011. Photograph: Jerome A Pollos/AP

blocks.text: But advocates view the continuing trend as more worrisome in light of Donald Trump’s recent moves against wolves. In September, Trump signed an executive order encouraging the interior department to consider stripping gray wolves of their Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections across the continental United States – despite the fact that ESA protections for gray wolves remain tied up in federal litigation.
At the signing ceremony, Trump appeared to ask an Arizona rancher whether his new order allowed people to kill Mexican gray wolves, a sub-species in the south-west that is also federally protected.
“You can shoot them as of today?” Trump asked.

The crowd laughed. US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins responded that interior secretary Doug Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes” – despite the fact that Mexican gray wolves remain ESA-protected and have not come close to meeting de-listing requirements.
Another rancher at the ceremony told Trump about his struggles with wolves in the state of Washington.
“You’re allowed to go and take care of it,” Trump said.
“If you say so, sir,” the rancher responded.
“We have no choice,” Trump said. “I’ve been hearing about it for a long time.”

“Trump says you can go out and kill wolves now – how many people took him at his word?” said Fahy, the wolf advocate. “These are sentient creatures. They’re basically dogs. They form family bonds. They mate for life, pretty much. They have a pack structure that is very similar to our social structure. How could we be so wantonly cruel to something that is so similar to us?”

articles.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".

blocks.text: A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to life in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 27 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
Ahead of sentencing, prosecutors in the court in Mombasa had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie because of the gravity of the crimes.
The prosecutors also cited what they described as Mackenzie's lack of remorse for the crimes. They requested life sentences for his co-accused.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives in Shakahola forest, including two grandchildren, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused have formally pleaded for mercy and asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Diana Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen", says Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.

Wanje says a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.
Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

articles.title: Solar for whom? What Philippines can learn from Pakistan’s rooftop boom
articles.summary: As rooftop solar begins to catch on in the Philippines, Pakistan shows why the country must make sure the boom reaches more Filipinos without leaving the power grid struggling to keep up

blocks.text: From above, Lahore appears to have changed one roof at a time.

Satellite images of the Pakistani city showed mostly bare concrete in 2021. Three years later, blue-black solar panels started covering roof after roof, in some neighborhoods almost forming a second skin over the city.
The change did not stop with wealthy subdivisions. Panels spread to farms, rural communities, even boats that had never enjoyed reliable grid electricity.

The Philippines is nowhere near that scale yet. But we’re already starting to see the same conditions that helped create Pakistan’s solar rush: expensive electricity, cheaper panels, strong consumer interest, and support from the government.

“Right now, the growth in solar rooftop is exponential,” Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) Chair Francis Juan told Rappler in a mix of English and Filipino. “Part of the reason is the electricity rates and retail rates are so high that if you have solar rooftop available, you invest in that installation, you will not consume from the grid.”

Juan estimated that consumers could save P13 to P14 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) while investment costs would only be about P7 to P8 per kWh. The time it takes to recoup your initial investment has also accelerated now that solar panels are cheaper and more efficient, shortening from five to seven years to as little as three.

ERC data also show that registered net-metered solar is already well beyond Metro Manila. Of 24,483 solar Qualified End-Users on the August 31, 2026 lists, around 18,500, or roughly 76%, were outside the National Capital Region, with particularly large counts in Pampanga, Cavite, Negros Occidental, Bulacan, Laguna and Rizal.

Those numbers are still small in a country with nearly 30 million households. But this growth is happening with incredible momentum. Net-metering registrations increased by 248.75% from August 2025 to June 2026, meaning the formal market more than tripled in less than a year.
That’s not even the full picture as these figures cover only those with certificates of compliance under the net-metering program, rather than every rooftop or distributed solar installation.

Utilities are noticing. Meralco estimated that rooftop systems generated 372 gigawatt-hours (GWh) for their owners’ own use in the first half of 2026, while its distribution sales slipped 0.5% from a year earlier.

Even Manuel V. Pangilinan — chairman of the Philippines’ biggest power distribution utility and of the company behind what is set to become the country’s largest solar farm — knows rooftop solar will make it big.
“It’s coming. It’s part of the technology trend,” he said of distributed solar at Meralco’s own H1 2026 briefing.
Yes, it’s coming, but the Philippines doesn’t have to discover and overcome every challenge on its own. Pakistan has already lived through it.

blocks.caption: What will it take for solar power to take off in the Philippines?

blocks.text: Pakistan’s rooftop boom didn’t begin with one sweeping government program. One might argue it took off because the economics tilted in its favor.

In Pakistan, electricity prices climbed 155% from 2021 to 2024, just as global solar module prices fell by roughly half. Not only was grid electricity becoming more expensive; it was also unreliable. Outages could last 8 to 13 hours a day, according to Khalid Waleed, a research fellow and energy expert at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute.
By the time solar really took off, the conditions had been building for years.
“Things were cooking,” Zeeshan Ashfaq, chief executive officer of Islamabad-based energy think tank Renewables First, said in a recent seminar. What followed was “bottom-up and market-driven.”

By June 2025, Renewables First estimated Pakistan had around 38 gigawatts (GW) of distributed solar, nearly as much as its utility-scale generating capacity. Yet only 8.3 GW was registered under net metering by December. Much of the boom was happening behind the meter, faster than official statistics could capture it.
The Philippines is still far from Pakistan’s scale, but a similar blind spot may be emerging.

Energy think tank Ember estimated Philippine rooftop solar may already have reached 1.3 GW by early 2026, nearly double the 721 megawatts (MW) estimate a year earlier by nongovernmental group Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities (ICSC). Nevertheless, it already suggests the ERC’s net-metering tally may capture only part of a much larger rooftop market.
In Pakistan, solar has spread beyond affluent households, but the way it’s used differs.

The country’s latest census in 2023 showed 26.4% of households in Balochistan — the vast, underdeveloped province bordering Iran and Afghanistan — reported solar as their main source of lighting. That’s much higher than the 12.6% in Sindh, the province which includes Pakistan’s economic capital Karachi, and just 2.2% in Islamabad, the national capital.
The contrast was almost the reverse for grid electricity, which reached 96.7% of households in Islamabad but only 57.1% in Balochistan.

blocks.caption: map visualization

blocks.text: Zain Moulvi, research director of the Alternative Law Collective, cautioned that high solar use in poorer and less-connected areas did not mean households were enjoying the same kind of systems as wealthier users.

In Balochistan and Sindh, many poorer households owned only a few panels, often enough for basic lighting rather than a full household system. Moulvi described these as “very small amounts of panels” providing “very minimal lighting.”

Financing widened the gap. Waleed said remittance-receiving households were about 44% more likely to own solar, while Moulvi said many poorer families and farmers went into debt to buy panels. A 2025 nationwide survey by the Policy Research Institute for Equitable Development also found a sharp divide in solar adoption, depending on a household’s financial situation.

blocks.caption: chart visualization

blocks.text: At the extremes, solar adoption stood at 38% among households spending up to PKR 15,000 (P3,403.07)* a month on electricity, compared with 88% among those spending more than PKR 50,000 (P11,343.58).

The Philippines faces a similar affordability gap. A May 2026 Pulse Asia survey commissioned by the ICSC found that 91% of Filipinos agreed that switching to solar would be possible if financing and more affordable payment options were available.
And make no mistake, the upfront costs remain quite steep. Current industry estimates put fully installed residential solar without batteries at P45,000 to P65,000 per kilowatt-peak (kWp).

blocks.caption: EXPENSIVE. Though the price has come down, industry estimates still put the total cost to install solar at about P45,000 to P65,000 per kWp.

blocks.text: Adding batteries for backup power costs another P150,000 to P400,000. Batteries rarely pay for themselves through savings alone, but may make sense where brownouts are frequent. A 5-kWp system also needs roughly 28 to 45 square meters of usable, unshaded roof space.

In high-rate areas serviced by Meralco, grid-tied systems can sometimes repay their upfront costs in three to five years, according to industry estimates. But that said, even the lower end of these prices is formidable compared with the Philippines’ P411,350 average annual family income in 2025.

Financing exists, but not for everyone. The GSIS Ginhawa Solar Energy Loan offers qualified government workers up to P500,000 at 5% interest. Banks have begun to offer solar products, but these tend to be subject to stricter credit requirements and favor much larger projects of 1 MW to 50 MW over small household installations.

blocks.caption: EXPLAINER: Is going solar affordable now?

blocks.text: For Ruth Yu-Owen, president and chief executive of renewable energy developer Upgrade Energy Philippines, the answer could be adapting solar financing into a format Filipinos readily understand: something akin to a postpaid mobile phone plan.

She suggested that distribution utilities such as Meralco and electric cooperatives could offer rooftop solar systems through installments bundled into monthly electricity bills, much like telecommunications companies bundle smartphones with postpaid subscriptions. This could make solar more accessible to households unable to afford the upfront investment, while giving utilities another revenue stream.

In fact, Meralco’s solar subsidiary, MSpectrum, already offers two residential plans with no upfront installation payment. One option allows customers to pay for the solar electricity they consume at P2 per kWh less than Meralco’s rate, although MSpectrum retains ownership of the panels.

Users can also go with a subscription plan that charges a fixed monthly fee, with ownership transferring to consumers after the contract ends. But this can be pricey. MSpectrum advertises a 5-kW system starting at P6,499 monthly over 10 years, adding up to P779,880. Over the years, that can be more than thrice as much the P225,000 to P325,000 estimated cost of buying a comparable 5-kWp system outright, though the subscription does include maintenance and insurance.

Meanwhile, neighboring Thailand is taking a more direct approach to affordability. On October 27, its government approved a 50-billion-baht program (P94.50 billion) to subsidize solar installations for 1 million households, offering 50,000 (P94,495) baht per person toward the cost. The program also offers access to financing and allows households to sell excess electricity to utilities at 2.20 (P4.16) baht per kWh.

Even with the subsidy, solar can still be heavy on consumers’ wallets. According to the Bangkok Post, a standard 5-kW system costs up to 140,000 baht (P264,586), meaning households still need to shoulder 90,000 baht (P170,091) after the subsidy.

Such a system could generate savings of about 1,800 to 2,200 baht per month (P3,402 to P4,158), but if a consumer needs to avail of government financing arrangements to cover installation costs beyond the subsidy, then they may have to pay an additional 1,200 baht (P2,268) every month over seven years – leaving actual savings of just around 600 to 1,000 baht (P1,134 to P1,890) per month while paying off the installation.
Pakistan’s experience also shows how regulators can make solar adoption non-disruptive by adjusting electricity rates, especially when rooftop solar grows faster than the grid.

At one solar-heavy grid station in Lahore, the Lahore Electric Supply Company supplied an indicative figure of 95 MW of registered solar capacity. But energy data firm Herald Analytics used satellite imagery and an AI-based geospatial model to estimate that around 177 MW was actually installed across the roughly four-square-kilometer area.

Utilities plan substations, feeders, and future power requirements around assumptions about how much electricity customers will draw from the grid. Solar-powered households rely more heavily on their own solar during the day, then return to the grid in the late afternoon and evening. If actual rooftop capacity is far above what planners assume, both the daytime drop in demand and the evening rebound can be larger than expected.
Pakistan was also carrying long-term take-or-pay contracts with large power plants, meaning fixed capacity payments remained even as rooftop users bought less electricity from the grid.

Waleed described this as a vicious cycle: high electricity prices pushed more consumers toward solar, but as grid sales fell, fixed costs were spread over fewer units, pushing tariffs even higher and making solar more attractive. Solar users also tended to return to the grid during the evening peak, when more expensive plants may have to run.

blocks.caption: [READOUT] The race to deliver cheaper power

blocks.text: Pakistan responded in February 2026 by changing its solar rules. Electricity they use from the grid is charged at the normal retail rate, while excess solar they send back after using what they need at home is credited at a lower rate.

Separately, Pakistan also adjusted fixed charges on electricity bills, so households still contribute to grid costs even if they buy fewer units of electricity because they already generate their own solar power. This helps ensure the grid continues to provide stable power to households when they need it.
Though the Philippines has not yet seen the same scale of disruption, the ERC is already planning for the same pressure points.

Chair Juan warned lawmakers in September that growing rooftop solar adoption could “cannibalize” the market of distribution utilities, eventually requiring changes to rate-setting and technical rules.
The ERC plans to revisit the Philippine Distribution Code after completing work on the 2026 Grid Code, including “appropriate interconnection standards” for larger rooftop systems.

blocks.caption: Cheaper PH electricity? Go beyond system loss; fix costly power contracts

blocks.text: The advantage for the Philippines is timing. As the country’s rooftop solar market grows, regulators still have time to make financing more accessible while ensuring grid rules and power contracts can keep pace before the boom leaves some Filipinos behind. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Exercise and cancer: What "living longer" really means
articles.summary: A major trial found more colon cancer patients were alive eight years after treatment with long-term exercise coaching. But what does "living longer" mean, and who does it apply to?

image.caption: Guided exercise can improve longevity after cancer by 7%Image: Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.
The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise than how to build it into routine care.
In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.
Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.
Does exercise improve colon cancer survival?

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025. Its 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.
Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half also met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway, but participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.
What does 'living longer' mean for cancer patients?
In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.
Here's what you need to know about breast cancer
Can exercise prevent cancer?

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the UK wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.
Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.
A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.
Could exercise help people with breast, prostate or other cancers?
CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide. "I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.
Why does long-term support matter for cancer patients who exercise?
The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.
"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agrees. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he said.
Do cancer patients get exercise support?
In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in ten had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

Campbell said, "there are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between." Good ones bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors. "Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."
What could exercise support look like in routine cancer care?
Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise, she said, engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "I think it answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.
Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.
A training session can bring structure and company, Nilsen said. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that."

articles.title: Supreme Court upholds law extending terms of barangay, SK officials
articles.summary: The same law also schedules the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections for November 2028

blocks.text: HIGHEST COURT. File photo of the Supreme Court of the Philippines.
Mark Z. Saludes
The same law also schedules the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections for November 2028

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC), in a decision made public on Friday, November 6, upheld the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 12326 or the law that set the terms of barangay officials and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) members at five years.
The same law also scheduled the next barangay and SK elections for November 2028.

Newly installed SC Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda, who previously served as associate justice, penned the ruling. It dismissed the petition filed by election lawyer Romulo Macalintal, which questioned the law’s constitutionality.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed RA No. 12326 last September 25. Apart from postponing the polls, the law also set the barangay and SK elections every five years after November 2028. It also limited the terms of barangay officials to two consecutive terms, while SK officials are limited to a single term.

In his petition, Macalintal said the law failed the requirements set in the ruling Macalintal v. Comelec in 2023, which allowed postponement of polls but only under certain circumstances, such as important, substantial, or compelling reasons.

But in the recent ruling, the SC explained that RA No. 12326 is a law that fixes the term of officials, not to postpone an election. It argued that just because a law fixes the term of officials does not mean it’s an election postponement law.

“The SC explained that the law’s main purpose is to increase the term of barangay officials from four years, as set by RA 12232 in 2025, to five years. It also reduces the maximum number of consecutive terms they may serve from three to two. Setting the next BSKE in November 2028 merely implements the new five-year term,” the ruling said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Crown stays murder charge against only accused in Sask. triple homicide
articles.summary: The Crown has dropped the murder charge against a woman who said she shot a man before he had the chance to shoot her at the scene of a triple homicide near Turtleford, Sask.

image.caption: The Crown has stayed the second-degree murder charge against Madison Jimmy. (Submitted by Jimmy family)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
The Crown has dropped the murder charge against a woman who said she shot a man before he had the chance to shoot her at the scene of a triple homicide near Turtleford, Sask.
Madison Jimmy would have argued self-defence if case went to trial
Madison Jimmy was charged with second-degree murder in the death of 28-year-old Tonio Cantell on Nov. 5, 2025.

From the beginning, Jimmy has said she shot Cantell in self-defence, after he killed her boyfriend and swung his rifle toward her and another woman. The third victim at the scene was another man who was shot by Jimmy's boyfriend just before that.
Jimmy, 26, then drove to Turtleford and turned herself in at the RCMP detachment in the community, about 210 kilometres northwest of Saskatoon.

Her case was committed to trial in June, after a two-day preliminary hearing in Lloydminster provincial court. On Oct. 22, the Crown issued a written stay of proceedings in Battleford Court of King's Bench.
Madison Jimmy's case was in the pre-trial stage at Battleford Court of King's Bench when the Crown stayed the charge against her on Oct. 22. (Hannah Spray/CBC)
Jimmy's lawyer Alora Arnold said the Crown called two civilian witnesses at the preliminary hearing, who testified about what they saw in the farmyard that day.
She said their evidence backed up the "very strong case for self-defence" Jimmy's defence was preparing to present.
"I think the Crown did their due diligence, we ran the preliminary hearing, they got to hear from other people who were there," Arnold said in an interview.
"The Crown took some time to think about things, and I'm sure it was not an easy decision, but ultimately came to the decision that there wasn't a reasonable likelihood of conviction."
Alora Arnold says her client feels like a weight has been lifted off her after the Crown stayed the murder charge. (Scott & Beaven Law Office)

The Crown consented to Jimmy's release from custody in August, on strict bail conditions that included a 24-hour curfew and electronic monitoring. Now that the murder charge is stayed, Jimmy is free without conditions.

CBC requested an interview with the Crown, but the request was declined. In a statement, public prosecutions said it is "unable to discuss the specific evidence or circumstances resulting in a stay," adding that the decision is not made lightly, particularly when there is a loss of life.
Arnold said that when she told Jimmy the charge was stayed, Jimmy was "understandably" very emotional.
"I know her first reaction was just pure emotion, and then … we touched base the next day and she's obviously very, very happy and feels this weight lifted off of her," Arnold said.
Jailhouse interview

Jimmy shared her story with CBC reporter Dan Zakreski in an exclusive phone interview two weeks after the killings. She was in the women's jail, the Pine Grove Correctional Centre, near Prince Albert.
She said on the morning of Nov. 5, 2025, she and her fiance, Dustin Roberts, had gone to the farmhouse where they lived near Turtleford.
They were in a truck with three people she knew casually — Cantell, who she knew by his gang name "DoughBoii," his girlfriend and another man, known to her as "Rboy."

items: Woman at centre of Turtleford, Sask. triple homicide says she shot in self-defence

blocks.text: She said after they arrived at the farm, Rboy shot a window of the farmhouse, and when Roberts asked him why he'd do that, Rboy pointed a gun at him.

"That's when my boyfriend reacted and he pulled out his gun and shot [Rboy]," Jimmy said. She said things seemed under control as they talked about taking the injured man to the hospital, but then Cantell shot Roberts.
Tonio Cantell died after he was shot on Nov. 5, 2025. (DoughBoii Cantell/Facebook)
Jimmy said Cantell's girlfriend was yelling at him, and she felt Cantell would kill his girlfriend and her.
"The look on his face," Jimmy said.
"He already shot my boyfriend, like, 'Who cares if I kill these two' kind of look, y'know? So I shot him before he could shoot us."

Jimmy said another man in the farmhouse who'd witnessed the shooting told her they should leave everything as it was, because all three shooting victims were dead. That's when the three survivors drove to the RCMP detachment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Owners of homes atop northeastern Ontario gold deposit in shock over a mine that may never be built
articles.summary: A mining company CEO revealed he was considering building an open-pit gold mine right in Virginiatown, Ont., leaving residents of the community of about 500 people in shock. "I do feel frustrated and…

image.caption: If Cadillac Mines proceeds with plans to build an open-pit gold mine in Virginiatown, Ont., it says it will offer to purchase some 250 homes to make way for the project. (Jimmy Chabot/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Sudbury

A mining company CEO revealed he was considering building an open-pit gold mine right in Virginiatown, Ont., leaving residents of the community of about 500 people in shock. "I do feel frustrated and quite worried," says one homeowner.
Cadillac Mines in early planning, feasibility phase for potential open-pit mine in Virginiatown

Residents of a small northeastern town are in shock and concerned about their properties after a mining company's chief executive officer revealed he was considering building an open-pit gold mine in the community.
Caitlin McAllister moved to Virginiatown with her mother, Pat Stephens, in January for its affordable housing costs and the promise of a quieter lifestyle.
They sold their home in Grey County in southwestern Ontario, and purchased a house and an adjacent property in Virginiatown, which has about 500 residents, for $50,000.

“We bought the property both so that my mom could retire and so that I could fund my education because we got a significant price difference between the house that we sold and the one that we bought,” said McAllister, who is studying to become a veterinarian.

items: Residents of northern Ontario town frustrated with proposed mine that would force them to relocate

blocks.text: McAllister said they have also invested another $20,000 in repairs and upgrades to the property.
They’ve enjoyed their time in the community east of Kirkland Lake and the freedom the low cost of housing has afforded them, she said.
“This was one of the most affordable places in the province that we looked at to live."
Residents packed a community centre in Virginiatown over concern about a proposed open pit mine that could force them to relocate. (Jimmy Chabot/Radio-Canada)
But on Sept. 29, a presentation from the mining executive upended their expectations for their future in Virginiatown.
Residents voice concerns at public meeting
Cadillac Mines CEO Rick Howes told investors that the company was considering an open-pit gold mine that would occupy most of the town.

"It's about 250 homes, 500 people. The town has been on a downhill slide since the mine shut down in 1996, so there aren't many services left in town for the people that live there," he said at the meeting for shareholders.
"There's not a lot of opposition as we talk to the community about moving the town."
Now named Cadillac Mines, the company purchased the former Kerr-Addison gold mine in Virginiatown in 2015. The site was actively mined for decades, starting in the late 1930s. It closed in 1996.
At a public meeting on Oct. 28, concerned residents said they felt as though they had more questions than answers about the possible mine.

“I want to be sure that I'm going to be compensated for my moving expenses, for my costs of my home, for the cost of all the repairs I've made to my home,” Stephens told CBC News after the meeting with a Cadillac Mines representative.
“And I would like to guarantee that I will wind up with what I have now, which is a mortgage-free property.”
Pat Stephens says she moved to Virginiatown to retire in a more affordable home, but is now unsure about her future there. (Jimmy Chabot/Radio-Canada)
Stephens later said that a $300,000 payout would be reasonable if she has to move to a community where the cost of housing is higher.
“I do feel frustrated and quite worried."
These were obviously comments that were not meant to hurt or to insult anybody. They were, I think, distasteful, and we're regretting them.Leon Leblanc, Cadillac Mines president-COO
“Cadillac Mines has made them the only possible buyers for any of the houses in Virginiatown,” said Steve Mallack.
At the Oct. 28 meeting. Cadillac Mines president and chief operating officer Leon Leblanc apologized for the CEO's earlier comments about a potential gold mine at the centre of the community.
“These were obviously comments that were not meant to hurt or to insult anybody,” Leblanc said. “They were, I think, distasteful, and we're regretting them.”
Leblanc said the company expects to have more certainty about its plans for a mine by mid-2027.
Quebec's lengthy mining displacement dispute
In 2008, a similar situation occurred in Malartic, Que.
Osisko Mining paid to physically move more than 200 homes and businesses away from a property that became an open-pit gold mine in the town.
Malartic resident Ken Massé refused to sell his property. After a years-long legal battle, a provincial tribunal ruled in the company’s favour and his property was expropriated.
Ken Massé's house was the only thing standing in the way of an open-pit gold mine in Malartic. Que. In 2010, a provincial tribunal ruled to expropriate his property. (The Canadian Press)
Shane Rayman, a Toronto-based lawyer who specializes in expropriation, said it’s rare for governments to step in and expropriate a property on behalf of a corporation.
“Sometimes the government will use these extraordinary powers to expropriate land to complete a land assembly that is necessary for what should be a very important economic interest,” he said.
Rayman noted there was a prominent case in 2005 when Oxford County expropriated land so Toyota could build its assembly plant in Woodstock, Ont.

items: Province to fast-track approvals for new gold mine in northeastern Ontario

blocks.text: Brent Doberstein, a professor at the University of Waterloo who specializes in climate adaptation and displacement, said that in a mining-related displacement, the company should be transparent with the people affected.

“There's no one single best practice, and I think through negotiation and discussion with the community and homeowners themselves, there could be a tailored process where each person decides what is the best approach."

Doberstein said it’s especially important that the most vulnerable people in a community don’t end up worse off after a move, and that the company involved works to avoid disrupting people’s means of earning a living.
“Wherever they end up moving to, they should be receiving an equivalent quality of life,” Doberstein said.
“So I think rather than focusing on housing values and dollar figures, you should be focusing on quality of life and quality of housing.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jonathan Migneault is a CBC News reporter based in Sudbury. He is always looking for good stories about northeastern Ontario. Send story ideas to jonathan.migneault@cbc.ca.
With files from Jimmy Chabot

articles.title: Turkey: Ex-minister arrested in a major fund manipulation scandal
articles.summary: Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a former deputy chair of President Erdogan's party, was arrested in a major funds scandal. The opposition claims Sayan Kaya and her husband cashed in shares worth millions in…

image.caption: Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya was a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip ErdoganImage: DHA

blocks.text: A former Turkish minister and senior official of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling party was placed in detention pending trial on Friday as part of an investigation into a multi-billion-dollar investment fund scandal.

An Istanbul court remanded Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya in custody on charges of "violating the capital markets law and membership of an organization established for the purpose of committing crimes," state-run news agency Anadolu reported. Her husband was released on condition that he regularly report to police.
Kaya served as family minister from 2016 to 2018 and until recently was a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP).
She resigned on September 26 following allegations by the Yeni Party, the main opposition party, that she had made huge profits from an investment scandal that hit the headlines earlier that month.

blocks.caption: Sayan Kaya rejected the allegations against her but returned some of the money she is accused of having fraudulently obtainedImage: Ozan Kose/AFP

blocks.text: Yeni Party Chairman Zeynel Emre has accused Sayan Kaya and her husband of receiving 2.17 billion lira ($43 million, €38.4 million) after reportedly investing 163 million lira in one of the funds, then selling their shares shortly before suspected price manipulation by investment funds triggered a stock market crisis that led the financial regulator to dissolve131 funds.
The couple denied any wrongdoing but have transferred some of the said money to an account designated by the banking regulators.
Opposition holds the government responsible

Erdogan's government has been scuffling with the blowback from the investment fund scandal that broke out in September. Prosecutors are examining allegations of widespread market manipulation affecting the savings of nearly half a million investors.

More than 430 people are under investigation over "suspected market manipulation and insider trading," including 112 who have been arrested as part of the scandal, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said this week.
Speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Ozel claimed that Erdogan was ultimately responsible for the scandal and called on the president either to resign or to take the country to elections.

Main opposition leader Ozgür Ozel said the members of the committee set up by Erdogan to deal with the fund crisis had themselves been detained as part of the same investigations. Mentioning Gurlek by name, Ozel argued that Erdogan should "take a closer look at those close to him."
