articles.title: Wild Horse Nine is a bleak, hopeless sign of the times. You're going to love it
articles.summary: Wild Horse Nine is Martin McDonagh's newest, bleakest outing yet. Starring John Malkovich as a dying CIA operative and Sam Rockwell as his hapless friend and partner, it also reflects a wider…

image.caption: Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich star in Wild Horse Nine, the new, depressing comedy from Martin McDonagh that seems to reflect a dour outlook rife in Hollywood. (Searchlight Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

Wild Horse Nine is Martin McDonagh's newest, bleakest outing yet. Starring John Malkovich as a dying CIA operative and Sam Rockwell as his hapless friend and partner, it also reflects a wider Hollywood theme.
Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich-led dark comedy about a dying CIA operative is a treat. Just not an uplifting one
It is the closing sequence of Wild Horse Nine.

John Malkovich sits in the passenger's seat of a little red car in a remote field on the remote Rapa Nui (more widely known as Easter Island). On the road ahead is a dead horse. Next to him sits the Chilean woman whose spine his gun has been pointed at for the entire ride.

The topic of conversation is how she might have thwarted an upcoming military coup in her home country. The coup that, in real life, saw the death of the world's first democratically elected Marxist president back in 1973.

The coup that, in the movie, Malkovich's CIA agent Chris Carlisle has helped plan — a crowning final achievement of a blood-spattered career soon to be ended by the terminal cancer growing in his gut.

Here are the ways that could have been avoided, Carlisle says, grinning through the morbidity like a (clinically) medicated Jack Sparrow. Her country could've elected a leader America approved of. Or she could've killed every man and woman in uniform she ever laid eyes on. Or, she could've spent her life slaughtering every child who ever expressed the dimmest bit of enthusiasm for militarism, camaraderie and authority before they had a chance to put on a uniform.

Unfortunately, even then she wouldn't have been successful, Carlisle sighs — a clownishly mopey admission that's both terrifyingly true and outlandishly funny — because no matter what she does, there will always be more of them.

"So what you do instead is find yourself a hut on a beach somewhere. Somewhere remote. Keep your back to the ocean and your eyes on the tree line. And wait there with a gun until they come for you," Carlisle says. The joke is that none of this is funny.
"You'll still die. But at least you'll die with the wind in your hair."
Rockwell and Malkovich shine
Sound pessimistic? Well, Carlisle would likely agree with you. Small in scope, grand in intention and harrowing in its honesty, Wild Horse Nine doesn't work much as a balm for troubled times.

Instead, as it follows CIA partners Carlisle and the frantic Lee Chesterfield (Sam Rockwell) on a bucket-list vacation days before Carlisle succumbs to his disease, it functions more as a comically, cosmically bleak buddy comedy.

And unlike movies like this year's sunny vibe-realignment Project Hail Mary or bizarrely upbeat Michael Jackson biopic Michael, it argues against handling hopelessness with hopecore. Instead, Wild Horse Nine takes your mind off your troubles by gripping the back of your neck, pointing you down into the abyss and waiting until you laugh.

items: Michael Jackson biopic turns up the music and mutes the controversy. What's wrong with that?
Ryan Gosling's Project Hail Mary is the 1st banger of the year

blocks.text: In terms of both the buddy and comedy aspects, Rockwell and Malkovich each shine. The pairing has already generated a wave of very credible Oscar campaign buzz for the smirkingly sad-eyed Malkovich, and to a lesser extent, his hapless partner in crime, Rockwell.

A sort of chronically depressed mirror of Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe's The Nice Guys emerges as Chesterfield begrudgingly carts Carlisle across the wreckage of his life. As he drags him through fields of impassive Moai (the Indigenous name for Easter Island's giant heads — a fact Carlisle nearly murders a group of tourists for explaining to him). And as he ferries Carlisle into, and frantically out of, even more disastrous conversations with bewildered locals.

Carlisle, who is also suffering from a dementia-like deterioration of his memory, can't seem to keep his mouth shut about the democratically elected prime ministers he's killed in Africa. Or even the Democratic presidents he's dispatched from grassy knolls in Texas.
While this sets us up for a sort of madcap comedy, it does so while assuming there's comedy to be had in acknowledging the overwhelming futility and uncaring cruelty of being alive.
Malkovich, left, plays terminally ill CIA agent Chris Carlisle, while Rockwell is his at-wits'-end friend and partner Lee Chesterfield. (Searchlight Pictures)

It's a strategy that British-Irish writer/director Martin McDonagh has already employed in his other cheerfully dour titles including Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, The Banshees of Inisherin and the iconic In Bruges.
Any passing familiarity with those largely beloved black comedies should highlight what's in store for audiences here.

And Wild Horse Nine isn't entirely original in its adherence to the tone of those movies. Recycle two killers on an offbeat holiday, as per In Bruges. Borrow the personal tragedy mined for defeatist, absurdist grief from Three Billboards. Shake with the odd-couple love story of Banshees. Voila: you have the formula for the charming — if somewhat suspense-free — aimlessness of Wild Horse.
Echoing a depressing theme in Hollywood
For an espionage caper, there's little mystery: We know who will die and — pretty much to the minute — when. Think less Jason Bourne, and more JFK.

But there's one major difference. As Carlisle grieves for both his own vitality ("She's life and I'm leaving it," he explains to Chesterfield about why a woman's kindness puts him into a tailspin) and the people whose freedom he spent his life destroying, Wild Horse Nine actually ends up far more depressing than a presidential assassination.

items: Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'
Tom Cruise is fantastic in Digger. You might hate it

blocks.text: It's a theme you'd be hard-pressed to avoid while watching anything Hollywood put out this year. There was January's dire tone-setter 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple, or Spider-Man: Brand New Day's continuation of Marvel's newfound obsession with nihilism.

There was the fictional apocalyptic climate-comedy Digger, or the four-hour Musk documentary that "jokingly" ends with the entire planet exploding. And on the horizon, Luca Guadagnino's Artificial: the OpenAI, Sam Altman biopic about AI ending all human endeavours and purpose. It was submitted to the Golden Globes as a comedy.

So with everything seemingly so horrible in real life, who exactly is asking directors to reflect it back to us in our escapism? If Wild Horse Nine's surprising success as both a comedy and overextended eulogy is to be believed, maybe it's because there's a certain comfort there. Maybe when staring down a metaphorical (or literal) barrel, there's no greater sense of control than to smile back at it.
Or maybe it's just that misery loves company.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: A mysterious U.S. army barrel washed ashore in Quebec. Why did it drum up anthrax concerns?
articles.summary: Quebec provincial police have confirmed that a barrel discovered on an uninhabited island in the St-Lawrence River does not contain active anthrax — ruling out the most dangerous possibility in an…

image.caption: A bomb squad, helicopter, drone and hazardous materials team were dispatched during the Oct. 27 police investigation of the barrel discovered on an uninhabited Quebec island. (Yoann Dénécé/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal

Quebec provincial police have confirmed that a barrel discovered on an uninhabited island in the St-Lawrence River does not contain active anthrax — ruling out the most dangerous possibility in an ongoing mystery.
Barrel's discovery spurs talk of anthrax spores, World War II and a top secret project
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 06, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
On Oct. 27, police responded to a call and descended on Île aux Canards, roughly 50 kilometres northeast of Quebec City, to recover the barrel.
A bomb squad, hazmat team, and helicopter were dispatched to handle the barrel with caution, and test samples from the container were sent to a military base in Suffield, Alta., for analysis.
“Because of the year of this barrel, because of the story, we could not take any chance before having the results back,” said Sûreté du Québec (SQ) spokesperson Audrey-Anne Bilodeau.
She’s referring to the inscription on the greyish-green metallic barrel that reads “Property Air Force U.S Army.” Its label indicates that it dates back to 1942.
The inscription on the barrel dates it back to 1942. (Matthew Joycey/Radio-Canada)

In a news release Wednesday, the SQ said the analyses determined the barrel contains a liquid “that does not pose a threat to public safety,” but police did not confirm what the liquid was or where the container came from.
So — how did this barrel spur talk of anthrax spores, the Second World War and a top secret project?
The answer: A months-long Radio-Canada investigation into its origins.
A nearby military anthrax lab

Christine and Sébastien LeBlanc discovered the barrel about two years ago on their private island in the Isle-aux-Grues archipelago, near Montmagny. They didn’t think much of it originally — until a book called Project N was published in March.

It’s the work of investigative journalists Vincent Frigon and Yves Bernard. They revealed that, on a neighbouring island called Grosse Île, there used to exist a top secret lab where the Canadian military built bombs filled with anthrax spores.
Vincent Frigon, left, and Yves Bernard are the investigative journalists who wrote about Project N. (Matthew Joycey/Radio-Canada)

Anthrax spores are a form of bacteria that are deadly when inhaled. Frigon and Bernard found that the Allied Forces wanted to produce a half million bombs with the bacteria to kill the populations of six German towns.

“During the Second World War, there were three closely kept secrets,” said Bernard. “The first: the atomic bomb. The second: the Enigma code — decrypting the German code used by submarines. And finally: Project N.”
They recounted how the production of anthrax spores began in 1943 in a lab on Grosse Île, and carried on until 1944.

By the end of the war, no bombs had been manufactured. But the journalists were able to track down Thomas Stovell, a former member of the military who was responsible for cleaning up the lab where the anthrax was produced.

Thomas Stovell, a former military member who worked in the anthrax facility on Grosse Île, supplied Frigon and Bernard with a picture of the lab from 1942. (Courtesy of Thomas Stovell/Canadian War Museum)
Stovell told Bernard and Frigon that his colleagues “took [the anthrax] out to the middle of the St. Lawrence and dumped it.”
Before they did, Stovell said the batch was mixed with formaldehyde to kill off the spores.

Inès Levade, a clinical specialist in medical biology, is one of the few people in Canada who works with anthrax today. She said that whether the soldiers were successful in killing off the bacteria would depend on how much formaldehyde they added.
“The only way to have an answer to that question would be to find the barrels and test them,” she said.
A national pattern of munitions disposal

The Department of National Defence refused a request for comment from Radio-Canada. In 2010, however, Bernard and Frigon say they were told by the federal defence minister that they had no information that would indicate that anthrax was thrown into the St. Lawrence River.
"They told us: 'We lost the documents. The only boxes with information about Project N were lost over the course of a move,'" said Bernard.
“Who’s going to believe that?”
Alex Souchen, an associate professor at the University of Guelph, specializes in the history of munitions disposal.
Before the barrel was tested, he said his first thought when he heard about the police operation on Île aux Canards was: “Nothing good could be inside that barrel.”
Christine and Sébastien LeBlanc with the barrel they found. Radio-Canada visited them in the Isle-aux-Grues archipelago in the summer of 2026. (Matthew Joycey/Radio-Canada)
Souchen explained that it’s not uncommon for historical relics from the Second World War to turn up in water.

“There’s millions of tons worldwide of conventional and chemical weapons that were put into ships and sunk or that were thrown overboard item by item,” he said. For soldiers, it was the quickest, most direct way of destroying large numbers of weapons during a global push for disarmament.

In Canada, Souchen said these munitions were largely dumped in Nova Scotia, but some were disposed of from military bases along the St. Lawrence River or as ships made their way back to Montreal to be sold off.

items: Police bomb squad responds to ancient barrel sighted near island in St. Lawrence River

blocks.text: He said that the historical records of what has been dumped by the Canadian military is thin, as they would have been legally destroyed at regular intervals over the last 80 years.

The emphasis from the military is not presently to disarm underwater munitions, though they are discovered regularly by fishers — something Souchen called "a very dangerous, very threatening situation that the government needs to do more to address."
He believes there should be more emphasis from the military to identify what has been dumped in the water and the impact it has on the environment.
“They’re not going out to these sites and monitoring them in the same way that other countries are doing,” he said.
Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty was notified of the barrel’s existence, and the SQ says it will now transfer it to the Environment Ministry for further analysis and disposal.
With files from Jacques Taschereau

articles.title: Global stocks plunge amid AI slowdown fears after Democrats’ midterm triumph
articles.summary: Asian and European markets follow Wall Street with sharp fall as FTSE down 1.5%

blocks.text: European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, with the FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, down 1.5%, or 166 points, at the start of trading to 10,615.

The pharmaceuticals company AstraZeneca opened down 2.8%, the biggest faller on the FTSE 100. Other big fallers included IAG, the owner of British Airways and Iberia, which fell 1.5%, after it missed profit forecasts in a trading update, and the miners Antofagasta and Anglo American.
Germany’s Dax index opened down 1.5%, France’s Cac 40 has dropped by 1.2% and Spain’s Ibex is down 1.1%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8% in early trading.
Despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.
after newsletter promotion
The Nasdaq Composite index, for example, is still up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

articles.title: Pope Leo sets off on 12-day South America tour
articles.summary: The pontiff will hold meetings and celebrate Mass in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, with the latter attracting particular interest. The trip will be the longest and farthest of his papacy so far.

image.caption: The pope took off from Rome's Fiumicino airport in the early hours of the morningImage: Filippo Monteforte/AFP

blocks.text: The plane carrying Pope Leo XIV to South America for the beginning of his almost two-week tour set off from Rome on Friday.
Following a 13-and-a-half-hour flight, the pontiff is set to land in Uruguay, where he will spend three days before heading on to Argentina, and finally Peru.
The 71-year-old US-born pope is recovering from a lung cancer surgery that took place just three weeks ago.
Latin America is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, for whom the pope is their spiritual leader. However, fewer and fewer people on the continent identify as Catholic.
What is Pope Leo planning for his visit to Uruguay?
Pope Leo's first leg of the tour takes him to Uruguay, the most secular Latin American country.
It was the first country in the world to legalize recreational marijuana use and has since legalized abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying, all against opposition from the Catholic Church.
However, the enthusiasm around Leo's visit has come as a bit of a surprise, with tickets for his prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium selling out in just two days.

blocks.caption: The pope is expected to express opposition to some of the more liberal policies enacted in UruguayImage: Lucas Aguayo Araos/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: The trip will begin with a meeting with President Yamandu Orsi, leader of a center-left alliance. He is also planning to visit the Casavalle neighborhood, which is notorious for its high rates of poverty and violence.
With the first papal visit to Uruguay since 1988, Leo will be hoping to reinvigorate the faith in a country where only a fraction of believers attend Mass.
What will Pope Leo do in Argentina?
On Sunday, Leo will cross over to neighboring Argentina, the home of his papal predecessor Francis, who, however, disappointed his native compatriots by never returning home as pope.
At the beginning of Francis's papacy, some 71% of Argentinians identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. By 2024, this had fallen to 58%.

blocks.caption: Leo will hope his visit makes up for the refusal by his predecessor to visit his home countryImage: Agustin Marcarian/REUTERS

blocks.text: Leo is set to meet with Argentinian President Javier Milei, who has come under criticism from the Catholic Church for his sweeping cuts that have hampered programs for the poor and needy.
He is also planning to meet with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives.
Pope Leo to return to Peru
The final leg of the trip, on Wednesday, will see Leo return to Peru, where he lived and preached for two decades.
There is excitement about his visit to Peru, with the pope planning to celebrate Mass in his old diocese of Chiclayo as well as in the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
The pope will also celebrate Mass in the former Incan capital city of Cusco before honoring Peru's indigenous population by traveling to Pucallpa in the Peruvian Amazon.
The excitement can be seen in the street vendors selling T-shirts and rosaries with his likeness, while bakeries have been selling Leo bread.
Peru has also seen a weakening of the faithful in recent years, with the Catholic population falling from 76% in 2013-2014 to around 67% now.

blocks.caption: Peruvian Catholics have shown particular interest in the pope's visit as a type of homecomingImage: Martin Mejia/AP Photo/picture alliance

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte 'saddened, very angered' by manhunt vs. allies, says Kitty
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte has expressed disapproval of what he perceives as efforts of the Marcos administration to go after his allies and supporters instead of addressing the needs of the…

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 4:41pm

Former president Rodrigo Duterte has expressed disapproval of what he perceives as efforts of the Marcos administration to go after his allies and supporters instead of addressing the needs of the nation, his daughter Veronica “Kitty” Duterte said.

“He is saddened and very angered by the fact that the taxpayers' money is being focused sa pagpadakop sa kanang mga kaalyado nato, mga supporters, instead of the more important things,” Kitty Duterte said in a mix of English and Bisaya in an interview posted on the Facebook page of Alvin & Tourism.
(He is saddened and very angry by the fact that the taxpayers' money is being focused on arresting his allies and supporters, instead of the more important things.)

“Like right now, may El Niño, ‘di ba (there’s El Niño, right)? And several other things like flood control projects, budgets for the more important things, for the needs, the basic needs of the Filipino people,” she added.
The Philippine government has raised a P50-million reward for the arrest of Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, one of the known allies of the former president.
Dela Rosa has been issued an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in relation to the drug war of the Duterte administration, which supposedly killed thousands of people.
He was the chief of the Philippine National Police at the time the controversial anti-drug campaign was implemented.
Duterte, meanwhile, is currently detained at the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands, while awaiting his crimes against humanity trial.
Kitty Duterte said that Filipinos should stand firm in their convictions in opposing the supposed injustices in the Philippines.

“All I can say is that now more than ever, we have to remain steadfast in our conviction and on our stand against all the injustices we are facing as a people, as a nation, because we are the only ones who can stop this,” she said.
“At some point, it will get too much. So it depends on us,” she added. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Bojie Dy, the unexciting Speaker whom Marcos can count on
articles.summary: Rappler takes an inside look into the speakership of Bojie Dy, and paints a picture of a man who holds the country's fourth top job yet contends with the limits of his power

blocks.text: The story goes that when Speaker Bojie Dy needs to talk to Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, or vice versa, it’s the 65-year-old Isabela gentleman, the country’s fourth-highest official, who goes down to the office of the President’s son, not the other way around.

It’s a peculiar visual, confirmed in private to Rappler by two congressional sources who have personal knowledge about the two leaders’ dynamic. “It’s the mountain that comes to Mohammed,” one of them quipped.

More than a year into his speakership, Dy has mostly avoided the weight of the scandals that crushed his predecessor Martin Romualdez. He enjoys a sterling reputation among his colleagues, and even clashing voices agree he’s a nice guy.
But he also carries the enduring perception of playing second fiddle to the son of the commander-in-chief.
His speakership comes with the mighty title. But is the actual power sold separately?

blocks.caption: Bojie Dy

blocks.text: Dy was not top of mind to become the new House speaker. By August 2025, it was becoming clear to Malacañang that the flood control fiasco had exhausted Romualdez’s remaining political capital, and he had to go.

Those initially in contention to replace him were Navotas’ Toby Tiangco, Bataan’s Abet Garcia, and Bacolod’s Albee Benitez. Garcia and Benitez reportedly did not pass the Palace’s vetting, while Tiangco had already publicly said he did not want the chamber’s top post.

Dy’s name only came up later, but the choice made sense. He already belongs to the President’s Partido Federal ng Pilipinas, and was even the first PFP lawmaker to be included in Romualdez’s deputy speaker roster for the 20th Congress.

He was also seen as nonpolarizing. He wasn’t angling for the speakership or seen as politically ambitious or selfish. The Isabela native was just returning to the House after spending 15 years as governor and vice governor.

Dy may have come from a political family that lorded over Cagayan Valley’s largest economy for decades — 16 relatives are currently in government — but he did not have the same connections that made Romualdez a powerhouse in Congress.
Dy, nonetheless, was obviously the safe choice for speaker by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., as both of their families go way back, and the two share the “Solid North” regional bond.
Dy’s father, the late patriarch of their dynasty, was a loyal ally of dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos. Dy was already active in the Kabataang Barangay (KB) during the Martial Law regime.

“Though he was from a very influential political family while I was from humble roots, we got along well because as always he was down to earth, kind, and soft spoken,” Caloocan 2nd District Representative Edgar Erice, Dy’s KB contemporary, told Rappler.
In 2016, Dy backed Marcos Jr.’s failed bid for the vice presidency, and again in 2022, when the dictator’s son successfully reclaimed Malacañang.
As speaker, Romualdez was always seen as the President’s reliable shield against any impeachment attempt. When his time was up, Marcos needed another loyal ally. Dy fit the bill.

“We see no basis that would justify the impeachment complaint filed against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.,” Dy said as soon as a petition against Marcos reached the House for the first time earlier this year.

blocks.caption: Who is Faustino ‘Bojie’ Dy, successor of Martin Romualdez as House speaker?

blocks.text: On Day 1 of Dy’s leadership in September 2025, he made a commitment to clean up Congress’ ranks. “We have fallen short,” he admitted.

Dy had two main tasks: calm an electorate frustrated with corruption in Congress, and ease the anxiety of lawmakers who feared they were the next target of the administration’s supposed anti-graft campaign.
Whether he succeeded in both is another story.

This was the height of the scandal, when dozens of lawmakers were being exposed for their alleged ties to construction firms that undertake public works projects for hundreds of millions — if not billions — of pesos.
Zaldy Co. Edwin Gardiola. Dong Gonzales. Chiz Escudero. The Dutertes. The Villars.

“Speaker Dy told lawmakers at the time, let’s trust the process. If you’re not involved and have nothing to worry about, let the process take its course,” Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez, Dy’s closest House ally, said.

blocks.caption: TRACKER: Public officials with links to government contractors

blocks.text: Dy oversaw the abolition of the small committee, a closed-door group that decided which budget amendments to accept even after the House had passed the spending bill.

The Dy-led House instead livestreamed budget amendment deliberations to show more transparency. But watchdogs it supposedly partnered with remained dissatisfied, and called efforts an “empty gesture.”

The House’s 2026 budget reportedly added P23 billion for public works. Dy’s district was a top recipient, with funding more than tripled to P3.8 billion from P1.1 billion. For 2027, public works allocations for his district stand at P3.1 billion.

“We were asked to sacrifice, yet their districts were the ones that benefited,” House Deputy Speaker Ronnie Puno, president of the House’s second largest bloc National Unity Party, said in March 2026, when he publicly criticized the House leadership over budget woes.
Puno’s callout of the Speaker underscored Dy’s limited power to give Congress a fresh start after the budget scandal.

blocks.caption: WATCH: Why the budget process of Philippine Congress is prone to corruption

blocks.text: When Dy became speaker, he retained all of Romualdez’s deputy speakers and added five more, inflating the roster. He also kept Romualdez’s budget chair, Mika Suansing.

Unlike Romualdez, Dy is not perceived as the epicenter of power in the House. It’s the President’s son, the 32-year-old Sandro, who has become an unstoppable force in the chamber, according to numerous lawmakers whom Rappler spoke with.

“If a congressman has needs for his district, they are more comfortable reaching out to Sandro than the Speaker,” one lawmaker from the majority, speaking on condition of anonymity, explained, citing Sandro’s direct line to the Palace.
“Sandro has become politically mature, unlike before when he played a more background role.”

blocks.caption: 2026 BUDGET. Speaker Bojie Dy and Majority Leader Sandro Marcos pose for a photo op with other House lawmakers after it passes the proposed 2026 budget in October 2025. Photo from Sandro Marcos’ Facebook

blocks.text: Another lawmaker said that Sandro, with all the power he commands, needs Dy and his candor to soften the message.

“There are some lawmakers who find Sandro to be abrasive sometimes,” the second source said. “Si Bojie ang taga-areglo, taga-masahe (Bojie is the one who smoothens things out and acts as a mediator).”
Kamanggagawa Representative Eli San Fernando recalled his lobbying efforts on the abolition of provincial wage rates. It hasn’t borne fruit despite support from Dy and over 200 lawmakers.
“The logical thing is for Majority Leader Sandro to schedule it for plenary consideration. But he doesn’t, because the Palace and the economic managers do not want to,” San Fernando said.

Senior Deputy Speaker Hernandez thinks the Speaker has more agency than what the public sees. “It is unfair to say that because the Majority Leader is the son of the President, the Speaker will lie low. The Speaker is just quiet, but the President talks to the Speaker directly,” Hernandez said.

blocks.caption: TRUST. President Marcos and Speaker Dy speak on the sidelines of a Palace event. Photo from Dy’s Facebook

blocks.text: Other deputy speakers speak positively of Dy, who is often described as “humble.”
“He is a good person, amicable and very down to earth. He is always available,” Deputy Speaker Benitez told Rappler.

“He goes around without a retinue of camp followers, and his office in the House is not a closed, exclusive private club of privilege, but open to all representatives and to the people,’” Deputy Speaker Raymond Mendoza said in a separate text message to Rappler.
The unspoken limitations of the title that Dy holds complicate any effort to leave a personal legacy.

His flagship initiative is LegisHear, a program intended to bring Congress closer to the people. It involves lawmakers going to the provinces to hear their constituents out and help shape future legislation.
But is the House under his leadership effective in its lawmaking function?
In the first year of the 20th Congress from July 2025 to July 2026, out of his 52 pet bills, President Marcos enacted only one — the resetting of the Bangsamoro elections.

Almost half of these proposals had already hurdled the House, but the Senate — plagued by infighting and leadership coups — has become a bottleneck. Many measures, even those considered a priority, were pushed to the backburner.

blocks.caption: Marcos ends fourth year with fewer enacted pet bills to brag about

blocks.text: These factors have left the Speaker little to no tangible legislation to brag about.

The stalled proposals include the House bills on freedom of information, much-criticized anti-disinformation, the widely welcomed travel tax abolition, institutionalizing the government’s social amelioration program AICS, and the diluted anti-dynasty legislation.
The Speaker’s Kalinga bill, meant to ease fuel-driven inflation, found no strong Senate champion. Of what good is a meritorious House bill if no senator will carry it across the finish line?
Rappler has written to Dy’s office, asking for a sit-down interview. It has not been granted as of writing.

blocks.caption: Bojie Dy, the unexciting Speaker whom Marcos can count on

blocks.text: These days, there has been loose talk of Dy being a strong candidate for the vice presidency, should Sara Duterte be convicted at the impeachment court.
Dy is said to have played a passive role in the entire impeachment saga, despite being head of the chamber that enabled her trial at the Senate.

Hernandez claimed that even Dy didn’t know the final tally on the day of the May impeachment vote, only that there were enough numbers to indict the Vice President. At the trial, Dy delegated the task of managing the prosecutors to Deputy Speaker Jayjay Suarez.
The Constitution states that when the vice presidency is vacated, the President shall nominate a replacement from among the members of the Senate and the House.
Dy has not publicly declared his intent for the job, and likely won’t. Even his closest allies call him a reluctant speaker who never chased the post many of his colleagues covet.

“I’m not endorsing anyone, but he’s kind. BBM will sleep soundly if he is the vice president,” Navotas Representative Toby Tiangco told Rappler, when asked about what he thinks of Dy as a potential veep.
“Whether he will be a good VP to the Filipino people remains to be seen but he definitely will be a good VP to the President,” Erice added.

The vice presidency isn’t Dy’s to lose in this world of what-ifs. For him to get it, Duterte must first be removed, rumored rivals (Chiz Escudero, Win Gatchalian, Tito Sotto, even Lito Lapid) must step aside, and he must be offered the post and accept it.
For a man whose influence has been doubted, maybe the idea that he is being considered, has the agency to say yes or no, and has the opportunity to be reluctant, is power in itself. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 2 at-large suspects in Bacoor shootout identified --PNP chief
articles.summary: Two suspects who remain at large following a shootout in Bacoor, Cavite, which left five people dead, have already been identified, Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio…

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 4:29pm

Two suspects who remain at large following a shootout in Bacoor, Cavite that left five people dead have already been identified, Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Friday.
In an ambush interview, Nartatez said police are now pursuing the two suspects who managed to evade arrest during the operation on Tuesday.
“Yung dalawa (Regarding the two at-large suspects), police are now hot on the trail of these two suspects. They were already identified,” Nartatez said in an ambush interview.
Five of the seven suspected members of the Gapos Gang syndicate were killed in the armed encounter with the Bacoor City Police on Tuesday in Barangay Molino.
The suspects were allegedly members of a robbery group that had been under police surveillance for its involvement in several robbery incidents and other crimes.
According to the police, the group had planned to enter a subdivision or residential area while posing as security guards.
The group allegedly intended to rob a businessman believed to be keeping valuable items and a substantial amount of money at his residence.
Police chased the suspects as they fled aboard a car and a motorcycle after they were spotted lurking near their target subdivision around noon. The sedan overturned during the chase.
Two of the five suspects killed in the shootout with cops were former police officers, according to the PNP.
Nartatez said investigators will also determine whether the suspects were involved in other criminal activities in the past.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Death a ‘distinct possibility’ in collision running and face-slapping competitions, inquiry hears
articles.summary:
Impacts in emerging contact sports are akin to coward punches and cannot be made safer with regulation, neurologist says

  • Get our

blocks.text: Collision running and face-slapping competitions have similar impacts to that of a coward punch or “king-hit”, with death a “distinct possibility”, a concussion expert has told a parliamentary inquiry.

A New South Wales inquiry is examining whether emerging competitions such as Run Nation, in which two players run at each other and collide at high speed, and Power Slap, where players take turns slapping each other across the face, should be considered combat sports to better regulate the safety of participants.

But neurologist Dr Rowena Mobbs, an expert in concussion and chronic traumatic encepalopahty (CTE), told the inquiry she did not think there was “any form of modification” that would make the sports safer.
“Collision running and Power Slap are worse than eye-gouging and should be deemed a king-hit, for death is a distinct possibility,” she said.

A 19-year-old died in New Zealand last year after suffering a critical head injury playing a tackling game believed to have been inspired by the viral “run it straight” challenge, of which Run Nation’s organisers have claimed their competition is a safer version, turning rugby league “hit-ups” into a sport.

The inquiry was established in August. In September, a NSW supreme court judge ruled Run Nation was a combat sport, upholding a cancellation notice for a Sydney event that month from the Combat Sports Authority (CSA) of NSW.
The event has been rescheduled for 28 November after the authority’s medical advisory board approved its permit. Power Slap has yet to host an official event in Australia.
The chair of the CSA, Darren Kane, told the inquiry on Friday he would prefer to see new combat sports regulated, with mandated ambulance and medical support staff.

“If it was a regulated event, there’d be all these systems in place, and the people would have accreditations, they would have done concussion training, there would be doctors mandated at the events,” he said.
“Whereas you have these unregulated things, it’s pot luck.”
Run Nation’s organisers have said their events include on-field doctors and paramedics.
The inquiry did not hear from organisers of either competition, but received submissions from medical experts, bareknuckle boxing and grassroots combat sports groups.

Petero Taremwa, the founder of Get That Guap (GTG) fight club, which hosts mixed martial arts, kickboxing and boxing fights without a promoter’s licence, said the cost of participation was a “serious barrier” to fighters, while organisers faced significant costs from “permits, insurance, venues, and medical services”.
after newsletter promotion
“We’re not here to dispute the importance of regulation. We’re here because we want a realistic pathway to comply,” he said.
Taremwa said there had been no significant injuries at GTG events, which “always had a nurse who is also our DJ, who looks at the fighters right after the fight”.

Under questioning from the inquiry chair, Labor MLC Sarah Kaine, Taremwa said he did not think he knew better than the CSA, but that the cost of on-site ambulances required under regulation was unreasonable for an entry-level organiser.

In her evidence, Mobbs said brain diseases in participants in football codes and traditional combat sports resulted from “subclinical concussions or silent events … when they add up to probably tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands”.

But she said the stronger impacts experienced in collision running and face-slapping competitions meant a lower number of impacts could “trigger off a neurodegenerative disease, for example, later in life”.
Mobbs said she did not recall treating any patients with injuries from collision running or Power Slap.
She likened the potential impact to that of a coward punch or “king-hit”, because participants could not defend themselves and strikes came “right in the key area where you have most impact”.
The inquiry is expected to report back in December.

articles.title: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
articles.summary: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.

blocks.text: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.
Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.
The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.
Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.
Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.
But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.
Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabaab controlling many rural areas.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.
In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.
The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.
The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary.
But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach.

The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.
Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency.
"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.
AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.
The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.

The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.
Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.
The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabaab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.

Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year, adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos not impeached, replaced by Sara Duterte
articles.summary: There is no vacancy in the presidency, nor is there any ruling or order from the Supreme Court that impeaches President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., allowing Vice President Sara Duterte to replace him

blocks.text: Claim: Vice President Sara Duterte will replace President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. after his impeachment. The Supreme Court (SC) also ordered Marcos’ arrest.
Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube channel named “PINAS NEWS INSIDER” with over 1 million subscribers posted the claim on November 2.

The video is titled: “BIG NEWS NAGDISISYON NA SUPREME COURT CHIEF & JUSTICES! VPSARA MAG TAKEOVER KANA LAHAT IKUKUL0NG NA?” (Big news! Supreme Court Chief & Justices have decided! VP Sara takes over now; all will be jailed?).
The video’s thumbnail claims the SC convicted Marcos, alleging he will face detention and impeachment. This allegedly cleared the way for Duterte to take over the presidency.
As of writing, the video has garnered over 81,000 views, 4,000 likes, and around 377 comments — many of which praise the High Court for supposedly doing its duty and refusing to be swayed by money.
The facts: Marcos remains the duly recognized President, while Duterte continues to serve as the Vice President.

Based on Article VII, Section 8 of the Constitution, the Vice President may only assume the presidency in four specific instances: death, permanent disability, removal from office, or the incumbent president’s resignation. None of these conditions have occurred as of writing.
Supreme Court’s power: Although the SC is the country’s highest court, the judiciary has no constitutional authority to oust an incumbent president.

Under Article XI, Section 3, the House of Representatives shall have the exclusive power to initiate all impeachment cases. Marcos may only be removed from office “on impeachment for, and conviction of, culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust.”

While impeachment complaints were previously filed against Marcos, these were junked by the House of Representatives in February 2026. The complaints were separately endorsed by Pusong Pinoy Representative Jett Nisay and the three-member Makabayan bloc over Marcos’s supposed role in flood control projects and overall national budget issues, and alleged drug use, among others.

The Constitution also states that no impeachment proceeding may be initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year. This means Marcos is constitutionally shielded from new impeachment proceedings until February 2027.
As of writing, only Duterte is undergoing an impeachment trial in the Senate.
Furthermore, an incumbent president enjoys immunity from suit, which protects him from criminal prosecution or arrest while in office.

Existing case: Marcos does face an existing legal judgment abroad, but not in the Philippines. The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed in 2012 a $353-million contempt judgment against Marcos Jr. and his mother Imelda Marcos.

The two violated an injunction that prohibited them from distributing assets meant for Martial Law human rights victims. The contempt judgment named Bongbong and Imelda as representatives of Ferdinand E. Marcos’ estate.
Lack of evidence: The video presents no verifiable evidence to substantiate its claims of Marcos’ impeachment or Duterte’s takeover.

Instead, the video strings together unrelated public footage lifted from past press briefings and public appearances of government officials from Malacañang, the Senate, and former chief justice Alexander Gesmundo.

Accompanying the visuals is an unidentified female voiceover offering commentary on Philippine political and budgetary issues. The narration cites decisions concerning the constitutionality of the General Appropriations Act, criticizes congressional budget insertions, and expresses dismay toward the current Marcos administration. None of these tackle the claims presented in the post.
Debunked: Rappler has debunked false claims regarding alleged criminal charges issued by the Supreme Court against Marcos:

items: FACT CHECK: No reports of SC order ousting Marcos
FACT CHECK: Supreme Court did not file charges vs Marcos over PhilHealth fund transfer
FACT CHECK: Supreme Court did not file charges vs Marcos

blocks.text: Fact checks were also published debunking claims that Duterte replaced Marcos as president:

items: FACT CHECK: No, Sara Duterte won’t be proclaimed president over Marcos health rumors
FACT CHECK: Sara Duterte did not replace Marcos as president
FACT CHECK: Sara Duterte not replacing Marcos as president following flood control protests

blocks.text: – Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com
Lyndee Buenagua is a Metro Manila-based journalist who primarily covers Bicol and Baguio. She is also an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

articles.title: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
articles.summary: Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November, satellite images suggest.
articles.byline: Shayan Sardarizadeh, Benedict Garman, Matt Murphy

blocks.text: Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.

Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.

The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.

A MAIAR analyst noted that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".

At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.

Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.

articles.title: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
articles.summary: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".

blocks.text: Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".

Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.

Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.

Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.

He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".

Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.

Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.

Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

articles.title: Did a data centre revolt affect the US mid-term election results?
articles.summary: BBC Verify examines whether US voters were influenced by the data centre boom - and the impact anti-AI sentiment could have on the industry.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondent

A US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.
BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.
What did the voter poll suggest?

The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.
The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.

This follows other recent Pew Research polling, external which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.
The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.
However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered "crucial or major factors" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).
Did the AI backlash affect Senate races?
But other factors would also have been motivating voters in these states, as elsewhere.

BBC Verify analysis of state-level voter polling for Senate elections suggests states which swung to the Democrats either followed the national trend over data centre concerns, or seemed less concerned.
So we can't say how many votes or Senate seats were directly delivered by data centre opposition.

But it's notable that three key states in the US AI build-out, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all elected Democrats as senators and governors who called for tighter regulation on data centres in one form or another.
These proposals include:

items: temporary bans on construction
ending tax breaks
requirements to fully cover their own energy and water infrastructure costs
mandates to use unionised construction workers
stricter environmental and transparency safeguards
local rights to veto

blocks.text: What could the election results mean for the future of the AI boom?
The US economy has been heavily supported in recent years by massive corporate investments in AI, external, including for data centre construction.

Official data, external shows inflation-adjusted monthly spending on building data centres, excluding the IT hardware to go into them, in August 2026 was $5bn (£4.2bn) - five times higher than in 2023.

Analysis by Columbia Business School, external suggests AI infrastructure investment in the US is currently larger as a share of the overall economy than spending on new railways was at the height of that boom in the 19th Century.

Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank, told BBC Verify the industry should anticipate that new state leaders will put conditions on or "even stop runaway data centre build".

Seema Shah, from global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said requirements for developers to pay for additional investment in the electricity grid, meet tougher standards over their usage of resources like water, or give up tax incentives could "raise development costs and slow new supply".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Stargate Oracle AI data centre spans roughly four million square feet in Abilene, Texas

blocks.text: The Stargate Oracle AI data centre spans roughly four million square feet in Abilene, Texas
However, Heather West from the Eurasia Group consultancy said temporary bans on construction and new regulations might delay the data centre roll out, but would not stop it entirely.

She said "projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed", but delays would affect the "next wave" of building through "local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centres pay for their own power".

Analysts from the consultancy Oxford Economics have said there are also strong economic incentives for politicians to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction, pointing to tax revenue and construction jobs they bring.

Deepak Surana of the Futurum Group, a technology research firm, said he expected there would ultimately be "a negotiation, not a moratorium" from Texas state leaders on data centres to ensure no negative impact on residents' energy and water bills.
OpenAI, which has a data centre in Texas and under-construction projects in Ohio, pledged to ensure it fully paid for its own electricity on Thursday, external - one day after the midterm results.
Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett

articles.title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
articles.summary: Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the village of Bédar this summer.

blocks.text: Families of Britons killed in Spain wildfires demand answers
ByNick Beake
Europe correspondent
Relatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.
Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.
Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in.
"If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.
He lost his father Michael and his dad's partner Christine.

The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.
The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.
The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.
Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe.
"It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.
The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.
'Issue the damned alert!'
Michael Chard built his house in Bédar from scratch. "He called it Casa Micas," his son said. "It was his place in the sun, it was his little paradise."
On the morning of the fire, Michael's partner Christine had met friends and was due to go to the hairdresser. "Then everything changed... the whole world changed for them," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Christine and Michael Chard are among the 15 people killed in July's deadly wildfire in the village of Bédar

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy of the Chard family
Christine and Michael Chard are among the 15 people killed in July's deadly wildfire in the village of Bédar

Duncan Chard said his father, who had two artificial knees and walked with a stick, left his house with Christine as soon as they saw the flames. They left their phones and passports behind and tried to escape by car, but the road was blocked.
"This is an action of a brave person who was fighting to the end," he said.
Andalusia's emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, has said the region decided not to use the system that sends emergency alerts to mobile phones because it could not be tailored to specific communities.
Officials have said some residents needed to evacuate while others were safer staying in their homes. They also argued an alert could have caused panic and traffic jams.
The families reject that.
"Issue the damned alert!" said Chard. "Ring the bells, send the police guy out with his horn, go door to door, do everything."
Thomas-Wolf Verdonckt, a Belgian virologist whose father Stanislas, 63, died, was on the phone to him as the flames approached.

He says the victims "never received advice on what they should do, and certainly not warnings that they were in danger", and that the authorities' claim that everyone in the area was given adequate warning is not true.

"The only contact that the government managed to make with the victims was a couple of minutes before the flames engulfed everyone. One police car drove by with the sirens on. There was no talking, there was no messaging."

Bédar's emergency plan was last approved in 2019, and regional officials say it was in the process of being updated. The municipality is classified by the Andalusian government as being at risk from wildfires.

blocks.caption: Satellite map of south-eastern Spain showing the area affected by a wildfire near Bédar, inland from the Mediterranean coast. Dark brown and black burn scars are highlighted within a boxed area around Bédar. Nearby towns marked on the map include Los Gallardos, Mojácar on the coast, and Palomares…

blocks.text: Of the 15 people who died in Bédar, 14 were foreign nationals: nine British citizens, three Belgian, one French and one American. The other victim was Spanish.
In the days after the fire, Sanz faced a backlash for appearing to blame the victims. He said some people who made the decision to leave "at the last minute, took the wrong path".
Verdonckt has been trying to find answers ever since the blaze.
"The morning afterwards, the Spanish officials brought out... a version of events which was simply the complete opposite of what I experienced," he said.
He also believes a public inquiry is needed to prevent a similar disaster happening in Spain in the future.
"They are putting the safety of citizens in second place. That's simply not okay."
'A huge hole in our lives'
Danni Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, lost her parents Pete and Fran in the fire.
They had lived in Bédar since 2018. Fran, a former headteacher, ran a quiz night that raised money for the local school and church.
"They were fantastic parents, my biggest champions and cheerleaders," said Danni. "They leave a huge, huge hole in our lives."
She says her mother texted her at about 19:00 to say they had packed in case they had to leave.
"They were waiting for instructions, and those instructions didn't come," she said.
Her parents died on the part of Bédar known as English Hill, one of the places where, families say, the authorities' only contact came minutes before the flames arrived.
Gillam-Kirton says her grief has been made worse by the way the Spanish authorities have behaved since.
Local police had told the family that Pete and Fran's car had been "meticulously searched" by forensic specialists and that she would find nothing.

But in August, a month afterwards, Gillam-Kirton and her husband found what appeared to be human bones in the burnt-out car in which her father died. "I picked up what I recognised to be... part of a pelvis or a hip joint," she said.
Gillam-Kirton fears they were her father's remains.
Within minutes they also found her parents' mobile phones, jewellery, house keys and money. Police had earlier told the family that no personal belongings had survived.
Spain's Guardia Civil police have been approached for comment.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Danni Gillam-Kirton says she found human bones and her parents' possessions in the burnt-out shell of their car

blocks.text: Image source, Danni Gillam-Kirton
Danni Gillam-Kirton says she found human bones and her parents' possessions in the burnt-out shell of their car
The fragments were eventually sent to Madrid for testing. The family says police have now told them no DNA was recovered and that the bones were those of an animal.
But Gillam-Kirton says experts, including a forensic anthropologist who worked on the Grenfell Tower fire investigation, believe the fragments were human.
"We still don't know who or what they are," she said.

Gillam-Kirton complained to the Guardia Civil. She says the reply told her only that the matter had been passed to the courts, and offered condolences for "the death of your relative", in the singular, when in fact she had lost both her parents.
"It feels like they're going to hope that we exhaust ourselves," she said. "Either the burden of grief is going to be enough for us to give up, or that we're going to financially exhaust ourselves."
Gillam-Kirton says there is "a real lack of empathy when you're dealing with families that have lost so much".
The one thing she wants above all is for someone to acknowledge what went wrong: "No-one seems to be willing to say 'do you know what, we made a mistake and for that we are sorry'."
The death toll in Bédar was the highest from any single fire in Spain during the summer of 2026, and one of the largest in the country's history.
Many victims were trapped as they tried to escape the village, as survivor Malcolm Timbrell told me outside his devastated home in July.
The cause of the disaster, also known as the Los Gallardos fire after the neighbouring town where it started, is the subject of a criminal investigation.
In July, the Guardia Civil said it was believed to have been started by a fallen power line, but that explanation has been called into question.

The BBC has seen a letter in which the Andalusian government refused a request from Socialist MPs for its official reports on the fire. These included any documents explaining why no alert was sent to mobile phones.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pete (far left) and Fran (far right) both died in the wildfire in July. Karen (second left) wants to know more about what happened to them

blocks.text: Image source, Gillam family handout
Pete (far left) and Fran (far right) both died in the wildfire in July. Karen (second left) wants to know more about what happened to them
The letter, signed by Sanz in September, said the documents could not be released because the criminal investigation is under secreto de sumario, a court order keeping the case file confidential.

Gillam-Kirton says the criminal case is focused on how the fire started, and that it will not necessarily examine the emergency response unless families pay lawyers to put that evidence before the judge.
"How can you have faith in these measures that they're putting in to mitigate future disasters if you don't know fully what happened the first time around?" she said.
"That's why you have a public inquiry," said Duncan Chard, "because the public need answers."
Families in the UK, Belgium and Spain have set up various support groups, as well as a website called helpbedar.com.
They have launched an appeal to pay for legal action, aiming to raise €100,000 (£83,000). Fundraising events are being held in both Spain and the UK, and so far about €11,000 has been collected.
Relatives say their fight is like David and Goliath.
"We are getting steamrolled by the Andalusian government," said Chard.
Ultimately, the families say all they want is answers, and for lessons to be learned so that others do not suffer the same ordeal.
They say they want their fight to be a tribute to their loved ones who died.
"I feel like this is all I can do for them," said Gillam-Kirton.

articles.summary:
Woman was shot on 14 December 2025 during Hanukkah festival and she has been in and out of hospital since

  • Get our

blocks.text: A woman who was shot during the Bondi beach terror attack has died in hospital almost 12 months after the massacre.
The 90-year-old woman had been in and out of hospital this year for treatment of injuries sustained during the attack on 14 December, a senior Jewish community source said on Friday.
The elderly woman had recently returned to hospital after developing an infection, where she died after having a stroke, the source said.
Her funeral was scheduled to take place on Monday. A family spokeperson requested “privacy during this difficult time”.
Fifteen people died after Naveed Akram, 24, and his father, 50-year-old Sajid Akram, opened fire at the Hanukkah festival at Bondi beach on 14 December last year. Forty people were injured.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon tells double murder trial shooting of Jesse Baird wasn’t intentional but ‘it was my fault’
articles.summary: Former NSW police officer gives evidence for a second day after pleading not guilty to murdering Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon has said he is “guilty of manslaughter” but said shooting Jesse Baird wasn’t intentional, as he gave evidence in his double-murder trial.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon continued giving evidence at the New South Wales supreme court on Friday. He described the moment he shot Baird, at which point Baird’s mother, Helen, left the courtroom.
“As police officers we are trained to shoot people at the centre of body mass … I had a split second moment where I said drop the knife … It was just police mode now,” he said from the witness box.
“If I didn’t do that I was 110% going to have that knife driven into my throat. And Jesse Baird was going to be sitting in my position today.”

blocks.caption: Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird (right). Composite: Supplied/NSW Supreme Court

blocks.text: He told the jury about an occasion when he went to the Royal national park with a friend and shot his gun. At this time he was thinking of taking his own life, and he wanted to test how loud his gun was, he told the jury.
He says he fired it at a tree. “I was very aware of making sure the bullet didn’t hit any innocent person,” Lamarre-Condon said.
The court also heard Lamarre-Condon signed out his firearm for a shift, three days before the alleged murders.
He had permission to do this, he told the court, and on the way to work had stopped at East Village shopping centre in Zetland to get his car washed.
The former officer claimed in court that it was common for police to get coffee or stop off elsewhere on the way to work.

He said he was thinking of stopping at Paddington to get his belongings from Baird before the other man got home from work, which would have put him in the “exact same” position he was in today as his firearm was still in his backpack.
On the day of the alleged murders, the officer said he wanted to retrieve his surfboard, clothes and Cartier ring from Baird’s home.
He took his mother’s car, because he did not want to be recognised, and began driving up and down Baird’s street to look for his ute, the jury heard.
Lamarre-Condon then parked the car in a spot left by Baird’s housemate, he told the jury.

He claimed he did not want to come into contact with Baird due to a risk the other man could take out an apprehended violence order against him as Baird had previously asked him to “please refrain from contacting me”.
Lamarre-Condon told the court he had seen what he assumed to be someone’s delivery motorcycle: “As soon as I saw that I had an idea … I saw a hi-vis hooded jacket, waterproof long pants and gloves.

“This moment here … I wish that I didn’t do this … But I had the thought process that if I was to put on this helmet and outfit I could knock on Jesse’s door I would look like an UberEats driver without any verbal interaction with Jesse,” he said.
The accused claimed Baird’s room was empty when he entered the home and that he looked through some storage boxes in the bedroom in search of his clothes but couldn’t find them.
Lamarre-Condon said he was still wearing the motorcycle helmet and his firearm in a holster under his shirt, when Baird saw him.
“He started yelling, ‘we’re getting robbed, we’re getting robbed’ … He couldn’t see it was me because the visor was down,” Lamarre-Condon said.
after newsletter promotion
At this point he claimed Baird lunged at him.
Lamarre-Condon claimed he aimed for Baird’s right shoulder and discharged the firearm.
The two continued to struggle but the officer’s finger remained on the trigger, the jury heard.

They tripped over a storage box on the ground, which is when Lamarre-Condon “accidentally” discharged the gun, he told the court: “It was my fault … I am guilty of manslaughter… But it wasn’t intentional.”
The jury heard he dialled the emergency hotline to try to get help for Baird.
But when he looked up, he saw Davies, who he didn’t recognise him at the time.
The accused claims the other man had picked up his gun.
“It was pointed towards me at my chest and he said ‘I’m going to fucking shoot you’,” he told the court.
“I started lowering my body towards the ground: I said, ‘Please don’t shoot me, I’m not here to shoot you. I’m not a threat I’m not here to hurt you.’
“That’s when he raised the gun towards my head and said, ‘Fuck off.”
The former officer said police are trained to redirect gun muzzles when firearms are pointed at them.
“I saw the gun, he was holding it with both hands I thought fuck he’s going to fire the gun and that’s where my police training kicked in,” he told the court.
“My left hand would have grabbed Luke’s left wrist and turned it away … my other hand pushed against the forearm and then I pushed the pivot point of the left wrist away from me.”
Asked by the defence lawyer whether the gun went off, Lamarre-Condon says:
“Yes, during this motion. And it got Luke.”
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.
